abdicated: When a king, queen or emperor abdicates, they give up the throne on purpose while still alive, and pass it on to their heir.
academy award: Also called the Oscar: the most famous film prize in the world, given every year in Hollywood, in the United States.
ageing society: A country where a big part of the population is old, because people live longer and fewer babies are born.
amaterasu: The sun goddess, the most important kami in Japanese mythology. The imperial family was said to descend from her. Her main shrine is at Ise.
anime: Japanese animated films and TV series. The word comes from the English word "animation".
annexed: When a country annexes a territory, it takes it and makes it part of itself, often by force.
arquebuses: An early type of long gun, loaded from the front and fired by lighting gunpowder with a slow-burning cord. Slow to load, but powerful.
article 9: The article of Japan's 1947 constitution in which Japan gives up war forever as a way to solve conflicts with other countries.
ashigaru: Foot soldiers. During the Warring States period, huge armies of ashigaru fought with spears, bows and guns.
asuka period: The period from about 538 to 710, named after the Asuka area near Nara, where the rulers lived. Buddhism spread and a real Japanese state took shape.
atomic bomb: An extremely powerful bomb whose energy comes from splitting atoms. Only two have ever been used in war: on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
bakumatsu: "End of the shogunate": the troubled years from 1853 to 1868, between the arrival of Perry and the fall of the Tokugawa.
biwa: A Japanese lute with a short neck and four or five strings, played with a large pick. Blind storytellers used it to sing The Tale of the Heike.
bronze: A metal made by mixing copper and tin. It is harder than copper and was used to make mirrors, bells, swords and statues.
bubble economy: The period at the end of the 1980s when prices of land and shares in Japan rose much higher than their real value, before crashing in 1990–1991.
buddha: "The Awakened One": the title of Siddhartha Gautama, a prince from India who lived about 2,500 years ago and founded Buddhism.
buddhism: A religion founded in India by the Buddha. It teaches kindness, wisdom and meditation as the way to be freed from suffering. It came to Japan from Korea.
bullet train: The nickname given abroad to the Shinkansen, because of its rounded nose and its speed.
bunraku: Japanese puppet theatre. Each big puppet is moved by three puppeteers in full view, with a narrator and a shamisen player.
burial mound: A big hill of earth built over a tomb. The largest ones in Japan are called kofun.
bushidō: "The way of the warrior": the code of honour of the samurai, with values like loyalty, courage, honesty and self-control.
chōshū: A powerful domain at the western tip of Honshu (today Yamaguchi prefecture). With Satsuma, it led the overthrow of the shogunate.
colonial empires: Groups of territories conquered and ruled by a powerful country far from its own borders, like the British or French empires.
covid-19 pandemic: A worldwide epidemic of a new disease caused by a coronavirus, which started at the end of 2019. Schools closed and people stayed home.
daimyō: A great feudal lord who ruled a territory with his own castle and samurai. The word means "great name".
democracy: A system of government in which the people choose their leaders through free elections and have rights like freedom of speech.
dogū: Mysterious clay figures made by the Jōmon people, often with big eyes. They may have been used in ceremonies or as charms.
dōtaku: Bronze bells from the Yayoi period, probably used in ceremonies to pray for good harvests. Some are decorated with little drawings.
earthquake: A sudden shaking of the ground caused by movements deep in the Earth. Japan has about 1,500 small and large earthquakes every year.
edo: The old name of Tokyo. It was a small village until Tokugawa Ieyasu made it his capital in 1603.
emperor: In Japan, the "tennō", "heavenly sovereign". Japan's imperial family is the oldest continuing hereditary monarchy in the world.
era names: Names given to periods of years, like Heisei or Reiwa. Today, a new era begins with each new emperor.
feng shui: A Chinese art of arranging buildings and cities in harmony with nature, taking mountains, water and directions into account.
fire whirlwinds: Spinning columns of fire and hot air, like tornadoes, that can form during very big fires.
five routes: The five main roads that started from Nihonbashi bridge in Edo and connected the capital to the rest of Japan during the Edo period.
fujiwara clan: A powerful noble family who controlled the imperial court during the Heian period, especially by marrying their daughters to emperors.
fukuzawa yukichi: A writer and teacher (1835–1901) who helped spread Western ideas in Japan and founded Keiō University. He appeared on the 10,000-yen banknote.
gekokujō: "The low overthrowing the high": when servants or vassals overthrew their masters, as often happened in the Warring States period.
genroku era: The years from 1688 to 1704, a time of prosperity when theatre, poetry, painting and city life flourished.
haiku: A very short Japanese poem of 17 syllables (5-7-5), usually about a moment in nature, with a word that shows the season.
hanafuda: "Flower cards": traditional Japanese playing cards decorated with flowers and plants for the 12 months of the year.
hanami: "Flower viewing": the tradition of gathering under blooming cherry trees in spring to picnic and admire the flowers.
haniwa: Clay figures placed on and around kofun tombs: cylinders, houses, horses, warriors, animals, like guardians of the dead.
hibakusha: Survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Many of them have spent their lives telling their story to prevent nuclear war.
hidden christians: Japanese Christians who secretly kept their faith for more than 250 years while Christianity was forbidden.
hiragana: A Japanese writing system of 46 basic rounded signs, each for a sound. Japanese children learn them first.
hiroshima: A city in western Honshu. On the 6th of August 1945, it was destroyed by the first atomic bomb used in war. Today it is a city of peace.
hunter-gatherers: People who live by hunting animals, fishing and gathering wild plants, instead of farming.
ice age: A long period when the Earth was much colder, and huge sheets of ice covered part of the land. The last one ended about 12,000 years ago.
indigenous people: The first people to live in a place, who kept their own language and culture, like the Ainu in Hokkaido.
intangible cultural heritage: Traditions recognized by UNESCO as treasures of humanity: things like dances, music, crafts, festivals or cooking.
jade: A hard, beautiful green stone. The Jōmon people made precious beads and jewellery from jade found in Niigata.
japonisme: The fashion for Japanese art in Europe and America at the end of the 19th century. It inspired painters like Van Gogh and Monet.
jesuit: A member of the Society of Jesus, a Catholic order of priests founded in 1540, famous for its missionaries and schools.
kabuki: A spectacular form of Japanese theatre with bold make-up, splendid costumes, music and stage tricks. All actors are men.
kaizen: "Continuous improvement": the idea of making small improvements every day. It is used in factories all over the world.
kami: The gods and spirits of Shinto. They can live in mountains, trees, rocks, rivers, animals or even in great people after their death.
kamikaze: "Divine wind": the name given to the typhoons that destroyed the Mongol fleets. The word was later used for suicide pilots in World War II.
kamuy: In Ainu belief, the spirits or gods that live in animals, plants, fire, water and even tools.
kana: The Japanese syllable signs, hiragana and katakana, created from simplified Chinese characters.
kanji: Chinese characters used to write Japanese. Each one has a meaning. Japanese children learn more than 1,000 at primary school!
karate: A martial art that developed in Okinawa, fighting with empty hands. It became an Olympic sport at the Tokyo 2020 Games.
katakana: A Japanese writing system of angular signs. Today it is used mainly for foreign words, like "terebi" (television).
kirishitan: The Japanese word for Christians in the 16th and 17th centuries, from the Portuguese "cristão".
korea: A country on a peninsula next to Japan. Many ideas, skills and people came to Japan from Korea, including Buddhism and writing.
kyoto: The capital of Japan from 794 to 1868. It is full of temples, shrines, gardens and traditional wooden houses.
kyōgen: Short comic plays performed between Noh plays, often about clever servants and silly masters.
lacquer: A natural varnish made from the sap of the lacquer tree. It makes wood shiny, waterproof and strong. Some Jōmon lacquer is 9,000 years old!
magatama: Curved beads, shaped a bit like a comma, made of jade or other stones. One is part of the imperial regalia of Japan.
manga: Japanese comics. They are usually read from right to left and exist for every age and taste.
meditation: Sitting quietly and focusing your mind, for example on your breathing, to become calm and clear-headed.
mongols: A people from the steppes of Central Asia. Under Genghis Khan and his descendants, they built a gigantic empire in the 13th century.
nagasaki: A port city in Kyushu, long Japan's window to Europe and China. On the 9th of August 1945, it was hit by the second atomic bomb.
nanban: "Southern barbarians": what the Japanese called the Portuguese and Spanish who arrived in the 16th century from the south.
naumann's elephant: A kind of elephant with long curved tusks that lived in Japan during the Ice Age. It disappeared about 20,000 years ago.
noh mask: A carved and painted wooden mask worn by the main actor in Noh. Its expression seems to change with the light and the angle.
novel: A long story written in prose, with invented characters and events.
obsidian: A black, glassy volcanic rock. When broken, it has edges sharper than a razor, perfect for making knives and arrowheads.
occupied: When a country is occupied, foreign troops are stationed there and control the government for a time, usually after a war.
okinawa prefecture: Japan's southernmost prefecture, made up of the Ryukyu Islands. It was the independent Ryukyu Kingdom until 1879.
paddy fields: Flat fields flooded with water to grow rice. They are also a home for frogs, fish and dragonflies.
paleolithic: The Old Stone Age: the very long period when humans made tools by chipping stone and lived by hunting and gathering.
parliament: An assembly of people who make the laws of a country. In Japan, it is called the Diet.
pilgrimages: Journeys to holy places for religious reasons. In the Edo period, trips to the Ise shrine were very popular.
pit dwellings: Houses built over a round or square pit dug in the ground, with a roof of wood and thatch. They were warm in winter and cool in summer.
prime minister: The head of the government, who leads the ministers. In Japan, the prime minister is chosen by the Diet.
prussian blue: A deep, bright blue pigment invented in Europe in the 18th century. It became very popular with Japanese print artists.
pure land buddhism: A form of Buddhism in which believers trust Amida Buddha to bring them to his paradise, the Pure Land, by reciting his name.
radiation: Invisible and dangerous energy given off by radioactive materials. In large doses, it can cause burns, sickness and cancer.
raised storehouses: Storehouses built on stilts to keep rice dry and safe from mice and floods.
regent: A person who governs in the name of a ruler who is too young, ill or absent.
ritsuryō: The system of laws and government copied from China in the 7th and 8th centuries: "ritsu" means criminal laws, and "ryō" administrative rules.
ryukyu islands: A chain of islands stretching from Kyushu toward Taiwan, including Okinawa. They have a subtropical climate and coral reefs.
samurai: Japanese warriors who served a lord. They were a ruling class for about 700 years, until the 1870s. The word means "those who serve".
sanshin: A three-stringed instrument from Okinawa, covered with snake skin, the ancestor of the Japanese shamisen.
satsuma: A powerful domain in southern Kyushu (today Kagoshima prefecture). It conquered Ryukyu in 1609 and helped overthrow the shogunate.
school system: An organization of schools for all children, with levels (primary, middle, high school) and a common programme.
self-defense forces: Japan's military, created in 1954, which is only supposed to defend the country. It also helps a lot after natural disasters.
shaman: A person believed to be able to communicate with spirits and gods, for example to heal, predict the future or bring rain.
shell mounds: Big heaps of shells and other waste left by prehistoric people. Archaeologists learn a lot about daily life from them.
shinto: The traditional religion of Japan, "the way of the gods". It honours the kami at shrines, often marked by a red torii gate.
shogun: "Great general": the military ruler of Japan who really governed the country from 1192 to 1867, in the name of the emperor.
shogunate: The government of the shogun, also called bakufu. There were three: Kamakura, Muromachi (Ashikaga) and Edo (Tokugawa).
shōwa: The era of Emperor Hirohito, from 1926 to 1989. It includes World War II and Japan's great economic growth.
smallpox: A very contagious and deadly disease that caused fever and spots on the skin. Thanks to vaccination, it has disappeared from the Earth since 1980.
soga clan: A powerful noble family in the 6th and 7th centuries who supported Buddhism and controlled the court for a time.
sonnō jōi: "Revere the emperor, expel the barbarians": the slogan of samurai who opposed the opening of Japan and the shogunate in the 1850s–1860s.
steamships: Ships moved by steam engines turning wheels or propellers, so they can travel even without wind.
sushi: A Japanese dish of vinegared rice with fish, seafood or vegetables. In the Edo period, it was a fast food sold at street stalls.
sword hunt: Hideyoshi's order of 1588 that took all weapons from farmers, so that only samurai could carry swords.
taishō: The era of Emperor Taishō, from 1912 to 1926, between the Meiji and Shōwa eras.
taishō era: The years from 1912 to 1926, a time of growing cities, new fashions and more democracy in Japan.
taiwan: A large island southwest of Okinawa. It was a Japanese colony from 1895 to 1945.
tectonic plates: Giant pieces of the Earth's crust that move very slowly. When they rub or slip against each other, earthquakes happen.
terakoya: Small private schools of the Edo period, often in temples or homes, where children learned reading, writing and arithmetic with an abacus.
tokyo: The capital of Japan since 1868. Its name means "Eastern Capital". It was called Edo before.
tsunami: A series of giant waves caused by an earthquake or volcano under the sea. "Tsunami" is a Japanese word meaning "harbour wave".
typhoon: A powerful tropical storm with violent winds and heavy rain, which hits Japan mostly in summer and autumn.
ukiyo: "The floating world": the world of pleasures of Edo towns, with theatres, fashion, entertainment and fleeting joys.
ukiyo-e: "Pictures of the floating world": Japanese woodblock prints showing actors, beautiful people, landscapes and legends.
unequal treaties: Treaties imposed on Japan in the 1850s that gave foreign countries special privileges and limited Japan's control over its own trade and courts.
unesco world heritage: A list of places in the world recognized by UNESCO, a United Nations organization, as so precious that they must be protected for all humanity.
unified: To unify a country means to bring all its parts under one single government.
united nations: An international organization founded in 1945, where almost all the countries of the world work together for peace.
vairocana: The "Great Sun" Buddha, a cosmic Buddha whose light shines over the whole universe.
waka: Classical Japanese poems of 31 syllables (5-7-5-7-7), used to express feelings, especially love and the beauty of nature.
washoku: Traditional Japanese cuisine, based on rice, fish, vegetables, soy and seasonal ingredients, beautifully presented.
woodblock print: A picture printed by carving it into a block of wood, inking the block and pressing paper onto it. It allows many copies.
world's fair: A big international exhibition (also called "Expo") where countries show their culture, inventions and ideas for the future.
yamato: The powerful court based in the Nara region that gradually united Japan. "Yamato" is also an old poetic name for Japan.
yoshinogari: A large Yayoi village in Saga prefecture, Kyushu, surrounded by moats and fences, with reconstructed watchtowers and houses.
yūgen: A deep, mysterious beauty that is suggested rather than shown, a key idea of Noh theatre.
zen: A school of Buddhism that focuses on meditation and simple living. It greatly influenced Japanese gardens, tea ceremony and arts.
